name: Dockside — incoming supplier paperwork agent for hardware teams
one_liner: For the supplier-quality / receiving owner at a 20-200 person robotics, drone, space or defense hardware company, Dockside is an inbox agent that reads every supplier shipment's document package (CoC, material test report, heat-treat and plating certs, dimensional/FAI report) against the PO's own quality clauses and drawing revision, and returns a one-screen "release / hold / chase" verdict with the exact mismatch cited — then emails the supplier the chase itself.
problem: Hardware startups buying machined and fabricated parts put documentation requirements on the PO (CoC, material cert to spec, special-process certs, dimensional or AS9102 FAI for new/changed parts), then receive a jumble of PDFs by email or portal download. Someone — often a quality technician, receiving inspector, or the mechanical engineer who owns the part — has to open each PDF and check: is the part number and revision right, does the lot/heat number on the mill cert match the one on the CoC, is the plating spec the one the PO called out, is the FAI actually for this revision, is anything missing. Public job postings at Neros, Star Catcher, SpaceX, Boom, Capella and Shield AI explicitly assign this document-review work to named roles, which confirms it is staffed, paid labour rather than a theoretical annoyance (sources below). Today the workaround is a shared purchasing@ or quality@ inbox, a Drive folder and a spreadsheet; parts either sit in quarantine while someone chases the supplier, or — the expensive failure — they get released and the gap surfaces later at an AS9100/customer audit or after a field failure when traceability cannot be demonstrated. Prototype suppliers make this worse: Protolabs' default "inspection" returns no measured values, Xometry's measurement/CMM/FAI reports are optional add-ons, and Fictiv requires material certs to be requested before order — so the paperwork a buyer assumed was coming often simply is not.
target_customer: Pays: a 20-200 person US hardware company (defence/space/robotics/drones, also medical devices) that buys custom machined, sheet-metal and fabricated parts from 10-60 outside shops. Buyer persona: the first quality hire — "Quality Engineer", "Supplier Quality Engineer" or "Quality Manager" — or, below ~50 people, the Head of Manufacturing/Ops who owns receiving. These roles are real and well paid: posted 2026 ranges include CesiumAstro $121-143k, Anduril $147-196k, Neros $154-215.5k (sources). Budget line: supplier-quality / QMS software, typically $5k-50k a year at this company size per a sector pricing guide (estimate, not audited).
why_now: Three things changed. (1) Document-understanding models are now good enough to read a scanned mill cert, a ballooned drawing PDF and a PO clause list and cross-match lot/heat/revision fields — a16z's 2026 Big Idea "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" (Jennifer Li, https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-1/) names exactly this PDF/screenshot bottleneck, and YC's "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (Brad Flora, https://www.ycombinator.com/rfs#the-15-an-hour-expert) describes the pattern of backing a non-specialist with AI to do specialist review work, which is what a receiving clerk doing SQE-grade paperwork review is. (2) The American hardware build-out — YC's "Robots Made in America" (Diana Hu, https://www.ycombinator.com/rfs#robots-made-in-america, 38,400 industrial robots installed in the US in 2025, up 12%) and a16z's "renaissance of the American factory" — means a growing cohort of young hardware companies hitting AS9100/prime-supplier qualification for the first time, which is the contractual trigger that forces documented supplier control. (3) On-demand machining is getting faster (tonight's bookmark: twentyfour26, YC F2026, ~48h turnaround, https://x.com/hemanthug/status/2117780769699733615) — when parts arrive in 48 hours but the paperwork takes a week of email chasing, the paperwork becomes the schedule.
comparables: GroundControl (gndctl.com, YC S2025, ~$3M seed, 70+ facilities, ~1,000 reports/month): the closest competitor. Automates AS9102 FAIR generation and has a "PO Review" feature that reads an incoming customer PO and flags quality clauses missing from the quote. Gap: it is built supplier-side — the shop producing the paperwork, not the OEM receiving it. Its Submission Hub is positioned for tier-1/2 package compilation, not for a 40-person drone company's receiving dock. | SmartCert (smartcert.tech, ~$2M seed via Aramid Technologies, 4,000+ companies claimed; pricing public: free Starter, $30 Basic, $199 Lite, $625 Standard, $1,199 Plus/month): a cert exchange network. Buyers can receive and request certs free, and it does flag missing data. Gap: it is a network — value depends on supplier adoption, and the free buyer tier caps automated email forwarding at 10 certs/month. It validates document fields; it does not reason from the PO's own quality clauses and the drawing revision. | 1factory ($75/QC user/month, 5-user minimum = $375/month floor): full supplier-quality and incoming-inspection module. Gap: it checks submissions against requirements a human already configured, per its own positioning; the five-seat minimum and QMS-shaped onboarding fit a certified manufacturer, not a 40-person startup with one quality hire. | Net-Inspect: aerospace FAI management, quote-only pricing, oriented to primes and their supply chains. | Nanonets / SAP Document AI / Artificio: generic document extraction for POs and quality certs — strong on OCR, no opinion about whether the package is acceptable. | Certivo: supplier certification/compliance checking (AS9100 status, expiry), i.e. qualifying the supplier, not grading the shipment. The uncovered gap: nobody sells the buyer-side, per-shipment verdict — "this package is short a heat-treat cert and the mill cert's heat number doesn't match the CoC" — to a sub-200-person hardware company at a self-serve price.
market_note: Estimate, stated as such. Global supplier-quality-management applications market forecast at ~$2.48B in 2026 (Future Market Insights); broader QMS software $11.7-13.9B. The relevant slice here is far smaller: assume 2,000-5,000 US hardware companies at 20-200 people in robotics/space/defence/drones/medical devices (my estimate — no reliable census exists), 20% buying something in this category, at $12-30k ACV for a focused product → roughly $5-30M of annual addressable spend as a beachhead, expanding into the far larger contract-manufacturer and tier-1 supplier base. Willingness to pay is anchored not on the software market but on labour: contract supplier-quality engineers bill $45-100/hour (2026 postings), and an in-house SQE costs $120-200k+. A product that removes 10-20 hours a week of document review is worth $1-2.5k/month on that arithmetic alone.
risks: GroundControl is well-placed and funded to flip to the buyer side — PO clause extraction is already built, and selling the receiving view to the OEMs their supplier customers ship to is a natural next move. | The buyer-side wedge may be too thin to stand alone: whoever owns incoming inspection usually wants nonconformance records, supplier scorecards and audit evidence too, which pulls toward being a QMS and into 1factory/QT9's price war. | Accuracy liability: cross-matching heat numbers and spec revisions out of scanned PDFs is the hard 20%; a product that is right 85% of the time still requires a human to open every PDF, which destroys the value proposition.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) That the receiving-side paperwork review is painful enough at 20-200 people to buy software for, rather than being absorbed by the quality tech who is already being paid. I found the role staffed and the workflow described, but I found no published statistic on how often supplier packages are wrong or how many hours per week this consumes — the single biggest unverified number in this brief. 2) That the clause-to-document match can be done accurately enough to be trusted: PO quality clauses are free text and highly company-specific, and a false "release" is worse than no product. The honest first version must be a triage that cites source text and routes exceptions to a human, never an auto-accept. 3) That a 40-person hardware startup will pay $1-2k/month for a workflow that is one person's partial job, rather than waiting until AS9100 forces them into a full QMS — in which case the budget goes to 1factory or QT9, not to a point tool.
first_customers: Ten named-type targets, all reachable without a sales team: (1) 20-80 person drone and defence-hardware startups hiring their first quality person right now — Neros, Star Catcher and Walden Robotics all have public 2026 postings that name receiving inspection and CoC/MTR review (job boards: jobs.nonlinearproject.com, greenhouse, jobs.nextview.vc), and a posting for this role is the single best buying signal; (2) 50-150 person space and satellite hardware firms one tier below SpaceX/Rocket Lab; (3) medical-device startups pre-ISO 13485 audit. Where to find them: the a16z American Dynamism, DCVC and Lux portfolio job boards filtered for "supplier quality" / "receiving inspector" openings — every such posting is a company admitting it has more incoming paperwork than people. Cold-email the hiring manager with "before you hire the second one, try this on last week's packages."
validation_test: This week, scrape the a16z/DCVC/Lux/NextView job boards plus Greenhouse/Ashby for 2026 postings at sub-200-person hardware companies containing "receiving inspection", "certificate of conformance" or "incoming inspection". Email the 25 hiring managers one line: "Send me last week's five supplier document packages and the matching POs; I'll send back a one-page accept/hold/chase verdict in 24 hours, free." Pass = 5+ companies send real packages and 3+ say the verdict caught something they'd have missed or would have taken them 30+ minutes to find. Fail = fewer than 3 send files, or they reply "our shops always send the right paperwork." Do this by hand with a model before writing any product code — the packages you collect are also the eval set.
build_plan: Stack: TypeScript + a document-capable frontier model (Claude or GPT with PDF/vision input), a forwarding inbox (Postmark/SES inbound), Postgres, a plain React console. No ERP integration, no QMS. Steps: (1) Intake — give each customer a dedicated address (acme@dockside.app); they forward or BCC supplier emails with attachments, and upload the matching PO PDF once per order. (2) Extract — per document, pull doc type, part number, revision, PO number, lot/heat/serial, spec callouts, dates, signatures, and keep a page+bbox citation for every field. (3) Requirements — parse the PO's quality-clause block and the drawing title block into a checklist of required documents and required values for that shipment. (4) Verdict — one screen per shipment: RELEASE / HOLD, each requirement green/amber/red with the cited source text for both sides of every mismatch, and a confidence flag that forces human review below threshold. (5) Chase — one button drafts the supplier email naming exactly what is missing or wrong, quoting the PO clause, and tracks the reply into the same shipment record. (6) Evidence — export the shipment's package plus the verdict as a single timestamped PDF for audits. Cut for v1: ERP/QMS integrations, nonconformance workflow, supplier scorecards, CMM data ingestion, mobile, SSO, any attempt to judge whether a measured dimension is technically acceptable (flag out-of-tolerance, never disposition it).
reasoning:
Dockside won because it is the only candidate where I could name the buyer, find that buyer being hired with published salary ranges in 2026, find the exact workflow written into their job descriptions, and show that every funded player serves the other side of the same transaction. GroundControl (YC S2025, ~$3M) sells PO-clause review and FAIR generation to the shop producing the paperwork; SmartCert sells cert delivery to the shop sending it and gives the buyer a deliberately capped free tier; 1factory's five-seat, $375/month floor and QMS shape fit a certified manufacturer, not a 40-person drone company with one quality hire. The receiving dock of the young hardware company is genuinely unserved. It builds on, but does not repeat, Promiseline (05 Nov) and Outbound/Sidecar: those chase schedule and price on the OUTBOUND side for job shops; Dockside judges the INBOUND document package for the hardware buyer, a different buyer, different artefact and different verdict. It also fits the builder exactly — inbox agent, document reasoning, TypeScript, no ERP integration, sellable in weeks.

Why it is a 7.2 and not an 8. I could not find a published number for how often supplier packages arrive wrong or how many hours a week this consumes; the one figure I found (30-50% of shipments missing lot-specific paperwork) is a vendor's own claim on 1factory's site and I will not lean on it. Pain is therefore 7.5 on confirmed staffed labour and confirmed prototype-supplier behaviour (Protolabs' default inspection returns no measured values; Xometry reports are optional; Fictiv requires certs to be requested pre-order) rather than 9 on measured cost. Timing is 7, not 9: the capability and the hardware build-out are real and recent, but no deadline forces a 40-person company to buy this month — AS9100 qualification is the trigger and it arrives company by company. Market pull is 7 because I found the role and its salary but no company at this size publicly buying a tool for this specific job. That is exactly what the validation test is designed to settle in a week, and if those packages come back with real mismatches, pain and market_pull both move up.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Dockside — incoming supplier document verdict agent for 20-200 person hardware companies. PICK. Named buyer with a salary band, recurring weekly workflow, incumbents all sit on the supplier side. 2. FAT Witness coordinator for data-center electrical gear (owner's rep schedules/documents factory acceptance tests) — FINALIST, dropped: research found the coordination is real (5-day readiness notice, dates fixed two weeks into manufacturing, FAT added post-award pushes delivery 4-6 weeks) but no evidence of complaints or an existing spend, and it sits uncomfortably close to Slotkeeper (07 Nov). 3. Permit correction-response agent for small residential contractors — FINALIST, dropped: PermitFlow (~$90M raised), GreenLite ($49.5M Series B) and Pulley already cover the workflow, and Backcheck (28 Oct) already took the correction-letter wedge. 4. Supplier-side cert package assembler for machine shops — dropped at screen: SmartCert ($30-1,199/mo, 4,000+ companies) and GroundControl own this exact buyer and workflow. 5. AS9102 FAI generator for shops — dropped at screen: GroundControl, InspectionXpert (~$125-235/mo), 1factory, Net-Inspect, CadNexa, Leo AI all ship it. 6. IDE/agent extension allow-listing and update-delay control for engineering orgs (from the Jack Cable guide bookmark) — dropped: too close to SkillProof (26 Oct), and VS Code's built-in extension policy plus MDM already cover the baseline. 7. Governance layer for Cursor-deployed live apps / vibe-coded internal tools (Retool reports 93% of senior tech leaders concerned) — dropped at screen: Retool, Superblocks, Dataiku and CSA are all actively framing this, and it is a crowded platform-vendor fight the builder cannot win from the side. 8. "Did the agent actually do it" mobile approval queue for non-engineering agent runs (from the DigitalOcean Cuttlefish bookmark) — dropped: DigitalOcean just shipped it for coding agents, and Doublecheck/Ledger (23 Oct) already cover agent write verification. 9. Plaid-for-benefits document wedge: one-upload income/residency proof pack for FQHC and community-clinic enrollment staff — dropped: strong YC signal but overlaps Frailty (31 Oct) in buyer, and a county-by-county rules problem is far past a weekend-and-evenings builder's reach to first revenue. 10. Vendor-security-questionnaire evidence pack for AI startups answering "how do you control coding agents?" — dropped at screen: Vanta already ships questionnaire AI and an agent; the differentiated slice is too thin.

PROJECT
1. Blastdoor — paste `code --list-extensions`, see what each extension can actually do + what changed in the registry since you last looked. PICK. Only candidate where a specific new public API (Open VSX version-changes feed, Aug 2026) plus a specific recent event (Cursor marketplace backdoor, 29 Oct) make it both newly possible and newly wanted, with a reason to return.
2. Interrogate — paste a repo, get quizzed on whether you can explain your own code (from Osmani's "cognitive surrender"). Dropped at screen: popquiz, cognit, commit-quiz and Sphinx already do it, and Ghostwritten in the library already pairs agent-authorship with a comprehension quiz.
3. Cooldown — paste package.json, see which deps are younger than Cable's 7-day minimum age. Dropped before research: straight repeat of Freshline (6 Nov) and adjacent to Strangers.
4. Teardown — photo of a machine → interactive exploded simulator, from the Claude skill post. Dropped at screen: Exploded is already in the library, and ExplodeView/ViNano/Teardown AI cover the neighbourhood.
5. Climbers — weekly leaderboard of fastest-growing startup X accounts, from @benln's screenshot. Dropped at screen: xpaiming already publishes a free follower-growth leaderboard, Social Blade dropped X in Mar 2025, and no free historical follower data exists — the dataset would have to start from zero.
6. Nagme — type "remind me to do laundry if it's been 5 days, 30 min after I get home" → downloadable Apple Shortcut, from @trq212. Dropped at screen: Shortcuts' own natural-language setup plus Fantastical/Todoist cover it, and generating a valid .shortcut plist in a weekend is a real unknown.
7. Localhost — paste a GitHub repo of an abandoned side project, get a one-screen "why this never shipped" card, from Cursor's "most apps never make it off localhost" line. Dropped at generate: funny once, no reason to return, and it mocks the user's own work.
8. Approve — a phone-shaped demo of agent approval requests, from the DigitalOcean Cuttlefish post. Dropped at generate: it's a mockup of someone else's product with no input the user supplies.
9. Firstrupee — a friction-free "what would ₹500/month have become" calculator, from @misbahspeaks. Dropped at generate: thousands of SIP calculators exist and nothing about it is newly possible.
10. Untangle — paste a file, get your leaky abstractions named, from @mazeincoding. Dropped at generate: explicitly cloning the project in the post, which the brief forbids.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3/3): summarised DigitalOcean's Cuttlefish (agent approval from a phone — informed candidate 8, then dropped), Jack Cable's November 2026 security guide via the ScottWu46 bookmark (npm 7-day package age, extension allow-listing, compromised Claude Code extension in Cursor's marketplace — informed candidates 6 and 10), and Addy Osmani's "Critical thinking when agents do the work" (no venture wedge; the cognitive-debt angle is already covered by Ghostwritten in the library). The twentyfour26 bookmark was checked for the manufacturing thread and confirmed as YC F2026 with ~48h turnaround on fitting parts.

Screening pot (6/6): one search each on AI permit/plan review (found PermitFlow/Pulley/GreenLite funding and expediter pricing — killed candidate 3), CNC quoting/RFQ (empty result), IDE/browser extension allow-listing (found VS Code's built-in extensions policy and Chrome/Edge MDM allow-lists — killed candidate 6), SOC 2 / AI-policy evidence (found Vanta already shipping questionnaire AI — killed candidate 10), vibe-coded internal tool governance (Retool's own 2026 report: 93% of senior tech and security leaders concerned — killed candidate 7 as a platform-vendor fight), and data-center FAT scheduling (the $14.2M/month-of-delay figure for a 60MW facility, but no software or complaint evidence — demoted candidate 2).

Deep research pot (12/12): spent on Dockside and the FAT candidate. Found AS9102 FAI vendor pricing and complaints (1factory $75/user/month 5-seat minimum; InspectionXpert OCR and GD&T complaints; manual FAI 6-8 hours typical, 8-40 QA hours wide range); SmartCert's full public price card and funding (~$2M seed, Aramid Technologies, 4,000+ companies claimed) and critically that its buyer side is free but capped at 10 forwarded certs/month; GroundControl's YC S2025 batch, ~$3M seed, 70+ facilities, ~1,000 reports/month, and that its PO Review is supplier-side; the 2026 job postings naming receiving inspection and CoC/MTR review at Neros, Star Catcher, SpaceX, Boom, Capella, CesiumAstro, Anduril, Shield AI, Rocket Lab and Walden Robotics with salary ranges; contract SQE rates of $45-100/hour; prototype-supplier inspection defaults at Protolabs, Xometry and Fictiv; and the adjacent email-agent market (Turian, Kavida/QAD Redzone, Microsoft's Dynamics 365 Procurement Agent, custom builds quoted at $12-30k). Two deliberate negative results changed the scoring: there is no published statistic for paperwork-defect rates per shipment, and no first-person engineer complaints surfaced — which is why pain caps at 7.5 and the validation test is designed to generate that evidence directly.

Sharpening pot (5/5): used across the two rounds above — buyer-side vs supplier-side positioning of each incumbent, whether anyone generates PO requirements from drawings (nobody does, confirmed across 1factory, Net-Inspect, CadNexa, InspectionXpert, Leo AI, Apriori), market sizing for sub-200-person hardware companies, supplier-quality job postings and salaries, and what tooling these companies use pre-QMS (no evidence of a standard stack; AS9100 is the contractual trigger, not headcount).

Investor signals weighed: YC's "The $15-an-Hour Expert" and "Robots Made in America" [latest], and a16z's "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" and "the renaissance of the American factory" [latest] all point at this candidate; I also considered and rejected "AI for City Hall" (candidate 3, blocked by funded incumbents and a past idea) and "Plaid for Government Benefits" (candidate 9, too far from this builder's reach to first revenue). No signal was used as the idea itself; each only lifted timing after the buyer was independently confirmed.
Sharpening (6.8 to 7.2): Round 1 — weak criterion: gap (6.5). The original candidate was "AI supplier-document checker for manufacturers", which sat squarely on top of GroundControl, SmartCert, 1factory and Net-Inspect. Change to the idea: flip sides — sell to the BUYER receiving the package, not the supplier producing it, and narrow to 20-200 person hardware companies rather than "manufacturers". Research (Perplexity on GroundControl's PO Review, SmartCert buyer-side pricing, 1factory/Net-Inspect buyer positioning) found GroundControl's PO Review is explicitly a supplier reviewing an incoming customer PO; SmartCert's buyer tier is free but caps automated forwarding at 10 certs/month and is a delivery network dependent on supplier adoption; 1factory requires five seats minimum at $75/user/month; Net-Inspect is quote-only and prime-oriented. The buyer-side per-shipment verdict is genuinely unclaimed. gap 6.5 → 7.5, and market_pull 6.5 → 7 on the back of the clearer buyer.

Round 2 — weak criterion: pain (7.0). Change to the idea: anchor the wedge on the one step with the most provable cost — not generic document storage but the cross-field match (lot/heat number, spec callout, drawing revision) plus the chase email, with an explicit refusal to disposition out-of-tolerance dimensions. Research (job-posting searches, supplier-quality contract rates, prototype-supplier inspection policies) confirmed the role is staffed and paid at Neros, Star Catcher, SpaceX, Boom, Capella, CesiumAstro, Anduril, Shield AI and Rocket Lab with 2026 ranges of $121k-$215k, contract SQEs bill $45-100/hour, and that Protolabs/Xometry/Fictiv do not supply measured dimensional data or material certs by default — so the gaps Dockside catches are structurally common, not hypothetical. What the research did NOT find: any published rate of paperwork defects per shipment, or first-person engineer complaints from 2025-26. So pain moves 7.0 → 7.5 on confirmed staffed labour, not to 8, because I could not find buyers paying for a workaround specific to this step. Average 6.8 → 7.2.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised the Cursor "Build Live Apps" changelog, Addy Osmani's "Critical thinking when agents do the work" article, and Jack Cable's November security guide (all three bookmarks had thin or empty text). Cable's guide is what produced the winning angle — "inventory installed browser/editor extensions, remove unnecessary tools, set a 7-day minimum package age" — and it also killed two candidates: the package-age idea is a near-repeat of Freshline/Strangers already in the library.
Screening pot (5/5): one prior-art check each on extension auditing, code-comprehension quizzes, X follower-growth leaderboards, photo-to-exploded-simulator, and natural-language-to-iOS-Shortcut. The quiz check killed Interrogate outright (popquiz, cognit, commit-quiz, Sphinx all exist and Ghostwritten in the library already quizzes). Exploded-view was killed partly by prior art and partly because "Exploded" is already a past idea. Follower-growth was killed by xpaiming plus no free historical data source.
Deep pot (8/8): Open VSX API surface (metadata, files, allVersions, download URLs, rate-limit headers, CORS uncertainty), Visual Studio Marketplace terms (restricted to Microsoft products — ruled out, Open VSX only), Open VSX coverage and the fact that Cursor proxies Open VSX for third-party extensions, existing paste-a-list tools (ExtensionAudit, vsxguard, ExtensionTotal, Agent Blast Radius, KillerSkills), the version-changes feed, and Open VSX 1.1.0's release date. What changed: the idea moved from "risk score" (crowded, and I can't honestly score risk from a manifest) to "capability inventory + what changed since you last looked", which is the gap none of those five cover.
Sharpen pot (4/4, 2 rounds of 2): see sharpen_notes. Net effect 7.4 → 8.1. Unresolved: CORS on the Open VSX .vsix download redirect — reason buildability stayed at 8 rather than 9.
Sharpening (7.4 to 8.1): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (6.5 at pick time; the pasted-list scan is a one-time audit, you do it once and never return). Change: added the Open VSX Registry Changes Feed as a second layer — "which of your extensions published a new version since you last checked, and which were deactivated or removed" — plus a localStorage diff on return visits. Research (deep pot, 2 calls): confirmed /api/-/version-changes is a public, unauthenticated, append-only feed of ACTIVE/INACTIVE/REMOVED version transitions with timestamps and cursor pagination, shipped in Open VSX 1.1.0 on 12 Aug 2026 and still marked Preview (https://blogs.eclipse.org/post/brian-king/evolution-and-integrity-announcing-open-vsx-110). Also checked prior art for exactly this: toolwatch (https://github.com/techdevfun/toolwatch) snapshots installed extension versions locally but its alerting is explicitly unimplemented, and no paste-a-list web tool layers the registry feed. Usefulness 6.5 → 8; freshness 8 → 8.5 (the feed is a specific, confirmed, recent capability rather than just "the news made this topical"). Caveat recorded: Preview status means the endpoint may change.
Round 2 — weak criterion: wow (7.5; a capability table is informative but flat). Change: lead with one sentence of counted powers ("7 of your 12 extensions can run a shell") and a red strip for anything the registry has since removed while it's still on your machine, with a copy-paste uninstall command. Research (sharpen pot, 2 calls): confirmed the removed-extension case is real and current — the trojanised Claude Code extension pulled from Cursor's marketplace on 29 Oct 2026 (https://www.ox.security/blog/malicious-claude-code-extension-cursor-ssh-backdoor/) — and that Open VSX's delete-vs-purge design keeps removed versions in the change log, so a client can detect "removed but still installed". Also re-checked that no existing free paste-a-list tool surfaces that: ExtensionAudit and vsxguard check removal lists but not against your pasted versions with a capability count. Wow 7.5 → 8; shareability 7.5 → 8 (the counted sentence is the card). Buildability held at 8, not raised: Open VSX CORS on the .vsix download redirect chain is still unconfirmed, so a tiny proxy may be needed — that is the one open dependency.
prototype_summary: An interactive Dockside prototype that turns a messy supplier-document inbox into a single receiving-dock verdict screen with per-clause citations, chase-email drafting, and an audited release-with-exception flow.
